issues.legal_issue: A right to receive a share of temple offerings is transferable and heritable when the duties attached to it are secular and do not require personal qualifications.
material_facts: The right to receive a share of offerings was subject to duties including arranging servants and visitor care, maintaining cleanliness, and meeting related expenses.
None of the attached duties was priestly or required personal qualifications; the duties could be performed by agents or servants at the holder’s expense.
issues.conclusion: The right to receive a share of offerings was transferable and heritable.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, a valuable property right to receive offerings is transferable unless prohibited by law. Where the right is independent of services requiring personal qualifications, it is also heritable. The Court approved Balmukand v. Tula Ram, AIR 1928 All 721.

rule.if: temple_offerings_right_dispute and right_carries_attached_duties and duties_are_secular and duties_do_not_require_personal_qualification

predicates.temple_offerings_right_dispute: The proceeding concerned a person's claimed right to receive a share of offerings made at a temple.
predicates.right_carries_attached_duties: The right-holder was required to perform duties in connection with receiving the offerings.
predicates.duties_are_secular: The attached duties concerned non-religious arrangements or services.
predicates.duties_do_not_require_personal_qualifica: The attached duties could be performed by agents or servants rather than requiring the right-holder's personal qualifications.

issues.definition: When a temple-offerings right carries secular duties that do not require personal qualifications, the right is transferable and heritable.

issues.legal_issue: A right to receive temple offerings coupled with non-personal duties is not a mere office analogous to a shebait's management role, but a property right capable of inheritance.
material_facts: The baridars received shares of offerings and had related duties, but the overall management of the shrine vested in a board of trustees.
The duties attached to the baridars' right did not require personal qualifications, and the right carried a beneficial interest in the offerings.
issues.conclusion: The baridars' right was not to be treated as a mere office; it was heritable property and could not be equated with a shebait's management role.
issues.legal_principle: In Angurbala Mullick v. Debabrata Mullick, [1951] SCR 1125, the Court explained that shebaitship combines office and property, duties and personal interest, and is not a mere office. Ram Rattan v. Bajrang Lal, [1978] 3 SCR 963, recognized hereditary shebaitship as immovable property. The baridars were not managers of the shrine in the way a shebait manages a temple.

rule.if: temple_offerings_right_dispute and right_carries_beneficial_interest and holder_is_not_shrine_manager and attached_duties_do_not_require_personal_qualification

predicates.temple_offerings_right_dispute: The proceeding concerned a person's claimed right to receive a share of offerings made at a temple.
predicates.right_carries_beneficial_interest: The right-holder had a beneficial interest in the offerings received.
predicates.holder_is_not_shrine_manager: The person holding the right did not have overall responsibility for managing the shrine.
predicates.attached_duties_do_not_require_personal_: The attached duties could be performed by agents or servants rather than requiring the right-holder's personal qualifications.

issues.definition: If an offerings right carries a beneficial interest, its holder is not the shrine's manager, and its duties require no personal qualification, the right is heritable property rather than a mere office.

issues.legal_issue: A custom restricting inheritance of a temple-offerings right to specified sub-castes cannot prevail over the Hindu Succession Act when the right is heritable property.
material_facts: The claimant was the daughter and heir of a holder of a share in temple offerings.
A custom restricted the right to members of four specified sub-castes, and the claimant had married outside those sub-castes.
The right was property coupled with duties that did not require personal qualifications, and it was not among the properties excluded from the Act.
issues.conclusion: The customary restriction was ineffective, and the claimant could inherit the right under the Hindu Succession Act despite not belonging to one of the specified sub-castes.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, makes inconsistent Hindu-law customs and usages ineffective on matters for which the Act provides. The right was heritable property governed by the succession rules in Chapter II and was not among the property specified in section 5 as excluded from the Act.

rule.if: temple_offerings_right_dispute and right_is_heritable_property and claimant_is_heir and custom_limits_succession_by_subcaste

predicates.temple_offerings_right_dispute: The proceeding concerned a person's claimed right to receive a share of offerings made at a temple.
predicates.right_is_heritable_property: The right to receive the offerings was a property right capable of passing by inheritance.
predicates.claimant_is_heir: The claimant was an heir of the person who held the offerings right.
predicates.custom_limits_succession_by_subcaste: A custom restricted succession to the right to members of specified sub-castes, and the claimant did not belong to one of them.

issues.definition: When an heir claims a heritable temple-offerings right that a custom limits by sub-caste, the custom does not bar inheritance.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant's failure to plead willingness to perform attached duties does not defeat the claim when the objection was not raised in the High Court and the claimant has not repudiated those duties.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the claimant had not pleaded that she was prepared to perform the services attached to the right.
The argument had not been raised before the High Court, and the claimant had not repudiated the obligation to perform the services.
issues.conclusion: The objection did not defeat the claimant's entitlement; the decree was to be understood as enforcing the right together with its attached service obligations.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the contention because it had not been raised before the High Court and because there was no repudiation of the attached obligations; the claim and decree were therefore to be understood as preserving those obligations.

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding was an appeal challenging a decree granting the claimant relief.
predicates.objection_not_raised_in_high_court: The opposing party had not raised in the High Court the objection that the claimant had failed to plead willingness to perform the attached duties.
predicates.claimant_has_not_repudiated_attached_dut: The claimant had not denied or rejected the obligation to perform the duties attached to the right.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a decree, if the objection was not raised in the High Court and the claimant has not repudiated attached duties, the claim remains enforceable subject to those duties.
